copy.body:
On July 16, Roblox launched Build — an AI tool that turns a text prompt into a playable game. No code required. Public alpha opens July 28.

That's not a small feature. Roblox has 132M daily active users, and Build just handed every one of them the ability to spin up a world without touching a single line of code. The 'can you build something in Roblox' question is basically solved.

Cue the panic. A recent GDC survey found 52% of game-industry professionals think generative AI is bad for the industry. I get the anxiety. But I think a lot of people are worried about the wrong thing.

Commoditizing world-building doesn't lower the bar for brands showing up in Roblox. It raises it. When anyone can generate a decent-looking space in minutes, 'we built a world' stops being a differentiator — it becomes table stakes, like having a website.

I've said this before, and it's more true now than when I said it: 'The tools don't exist yet. Brands can't just turn on a presence in Roblox like they do with Instagram ads. Every activation requires months of custom work. That's not sustainable. This is the infrastructure moment.'

Build doesn't fix that. It automates the shell, not the substance. The real gap was never 'does the world exist' — it's whether the presence talks back, remembers who's standing in it, and produces something a marketer can actually act on. Build makes more worlds. It doesn't make any of them remember your name.

Stop renting reach. Start owning it.

Let's talk.
